items.title: Report: Three newly created sites generated over 215,000 AI 'best software' pages cited by Perplexity across 380 categories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Three sites made 215,128 “best software” pages for AI. Perplexity cites them
items.summary:
A recent analysis found that Perplexity's AI models cited 7,534 URLs for software recommendations, with nearly 60% pointing to low-ranked or unranked domains. Three sites, all registered between December 2023 and May 2024 and apparently under common control, produced 215,128 machine-generated 'best software' pages that serve as a significant source for these AI recommendations.

These sites share technical infrastructure and content templates, suggesting a coordinated operation. The study highlights how AI grounding layers rely heavily on newly created, machine-generated content rather than established, high-ranking domains, raising questions about the quality and origin of AI-sourced product recommendations.

items.title: Mistral allows users and customers to opt out of having their input and output data used for model training across Vibe, Mistral Studio, and API services [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can I opt out of my input or output data being used for training?
items.summary:
Mistral provides users and enterprise customers with the ability to opt out of including their input and output data, such as conversations and documents, in the company's model training programs. The opt-out process varies by service: Vibe users can disable data sharing in their settings or admin panel, while Mistral Studio and API customers can manage opt-out toggles separately in the admin panel's privacy settings.

For Vibe, individual users are opted in by default but can opt out anytime, whereas enterprise customers are opted out by default with an option to opt in. On mobile apps, users can disable data sharing in the account settings. Opting out ensures Mistral no longer uses the user's data for training purposes, and toggles for different services must be configured independently.

The article outlines 14 technical hurdles, including the complexity of robotic hands, visual understanding, and task planning, which must be overcome to achieve broadly capable artificial workers.

The discussion emphasizes that current robot manipulators fall short of human dexterity and sensory integration, and that visual perception and environmental interaction remain difficult problems. It also notes that demo videos often showcase selective successes rather than consistent performance, underscoring the gap between public perception and actual robotic capabilities.

items.title: WebLLM launches high-performance in-browser LLM inference engine with WebGPU acceleration and full OpenAI API compatibility [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WebLLM: high-performance in-browser LLM inference engine
items.summary:
WebLLM is a new inference engine that runs large language models directly in web browsers using hardware acceleration via WebGPU, eliminating the need for server support. It supports streaming, JSON-mode, function-calling, and is compatible with OpenAI API, enabling local use of open source models with privacy and GPU acceleration.

The engine supports multiple popular models including Llama 3, Phi 3, Gemma, Mistral, and Qwen, and allows easy integration through npm, Yarn, or CDN. WebLLM also offers features like streaming chat completions, web worker support for UI performance, and Chrome extension compatibility, making it versatile for building AI assistants and interactive applications entirely in the browser.

items.originalTitle: ClickHouse vs. OpenObserve for Logs, Metrics and Traces (2026)
items.summary:
This article compares ClickHouse, a general-purpose columnar database, with OpenObserve, a purpose-built observability platform, focusing on their capabilities for handling logs, metrics, and traces. It outlines how ClickHouse is often used as a backend storage engine or directly for observability workloads, while OpenObserve offers native OpenTelemetry ingestion, unified querying, and built-in enterprise features.

Key differences include ClickHouse's local disk-based storage with optional cold tiering versus OpenObserve's native object storage architecture using Parquet files on cloud storage. OpenObserve supports native OTLP ingestion and cross-signal correlation, whereas ClickHouse requires custom ingestion pipelines and schema design. Additionally, OpenObserve provides built-in application-level RBAC and SSO, which ClickHouse lacks, requiring external solutions for enterprise access control.

The comparison also touches on high availability and scaling considerations, noting that ClickHouse's self-hosted deployments need additional components for replication and coordination, while OpenObserve's stateless compute nodes simplify scaling. These distinctions may influence organizations' choices based on their observability needs, infrastructure preferences, and compliance requirements.

items.originalTitle: The multi-agent architecture of 2026 was designed in 1975
items.summary:
The multi-agent architecture originally designed in 1975 for the HEARSAY-II speech recognizer is being revisited in 2026 through Mozaik, an open-source TypeScript runtime that implements agents communicating on a shared event bus. This architecture, based on independent experts collaborating without a central coordinator, emphasizes three core properties: concurrency, awareness, and adaptability, which together enable scalable and flexible AI agent interoperability.

Mozaik's design reflects principles from the 1970s blackboard and actor models, where agents operate independently, discover and communicate with each other, and adapt their behavior dynamically at runtime. The system is demonstrated in Baro, an autonomous software factory that runs multiple agents concurrently on a single repository, negotiating dependencies and adapting to changing conditions without blocking or centralized control.

This approach enhances parallel judgment and obsoletes traditional coordinators by enabling decentralized collaboration among AI agents. It revives and modernizes foundational concepts from early AI research, applying them to contemporary large language models as the new 'experts' within the system.

items.title: Analysis of HTTP headers sent by ten AI fetchers on a live site reveals varying identification and request behaviors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Which AI Fetchers Send Which Headers, Measured on a Live Site
items.summary:
A study measured the HTTP headers sent by ten AI fetchers including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Perplexity, Copilot, Mistral, DuckDuckGo, Claude Code, and OpenAI's Codex when accessing unique URLs on a Cloudflare Worker-protected site on September 3, 2026. The analysis compared these headers against vendor documentation, IP lists, and signing keys, revealing differences in how each fetcher identifies itself and interacts with the server, with some fetchers signing requests, others mimicking browsers, and some not making actual requests at all.

Key findings include DuckDuckGo as the only fetcher signing requests with a verifiable key, Grok sending browser-like headers from diverse networks making it indistinguishable from human visitors, and Gemini using undocumented user-agent strings from Google IPs not listed in official crawler ranges. Some fetchers like Perplexity and Copilot reported page results without sending requests to the origin server. These behaviors have implications for server-side bot detection and highlight inconsistencies in AI fetcher transparency and identification methods.

items.title: Researchers say AI can assist in planning bioweapons by aiding research and design but physical creation remains complex and requires specialized skills [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Can Help Plan a Bioweapon
items.summary:
AI can help with the initial research and planning stages of bioweapon development by retrieving detailed biological information and suggesting design modifications. However, the actual creation involves multiple complex steps such as sourcing materials, DNA assembly, organism cultivation, stabilization, testing, and deployment, which require hands-on expertise, specialized equipment, and tacit knowledge that AI cannot provide.

Studies indicate that while AI tools improve performance on individual virology tasks for non-experts, they do not significantly increase success rates in complete bioweapon workflows, which remain below 8%. The physical and procedural challenges, including the perishability of biological materials and the need for precise lab techniques, make bioweapon construction difficult even with AI assistance, limiting the likelihood of success without substantial experience and resources.

The Information has become the most trusted source on the AI business by breaking news about the biggest deals in the industry. Now we’re expanding that coverage with a new show called “AI Deep Dive” that will give you a more sophisticated understanding of the technology itself.

“AI Deep Dive” will complement our daily coverage with long-form conversations with the researchers and founders working on the frontier of AI.

I’m your host. I’ve written about AI at The Information for the past two years, taking advantage of my technical background to uncover and translate highly technical stories in AI and robotics. I studied computer science in college, briefly worked as a programmer and received a crash course in AI research while working at MATS, a mentorship program for AI safety researchers. These days I keep up with AI research in part by discussing a new machine learning paper every week with a reading group.

That experience sets me up to guide technical conversations with our guests. To kick off the series, I’ll be talking to Noam Brown, a research scientist at OpenAI, about the challenges involved in creating AI agents that can autonomously take actions on a computer.

Each of the following episodes will break down a hard problem on the technological frontier, from training AI models to control robots to studying the neuroscience of their “brains.”

As AI barrels ahead, bringing new developments every week, separating hype from real progress has never been more valuable. Understanding which technical problems have researchers stumped and what makes those problems so hard is the best inoculation against the hype.

TITV will remain our home for daily coverage of the biggest stories in tech. If you want to better understand the technology behind the business, I hope you’ll tune in when the first episode of “AI Deep Dive” airs on Sept. 14.

items.title: Why Regulators Are Scrutinizing Prediction Markets' Trading Arms
items.originalTitle: Why Regulators Are Scrutinizing Prediction Markets' Trading Arms
items.summary:
Fast-growing prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket are well known for their consumer apps, where people can bet on everything from sports and elections to the weather and stock prices. 

But those companies do more than operate consumer apps. Behind the scenes, several prediction markets operate their own exchanges and clearinghouses for the contracts, and some even have trading firms that make bets using the same contracts that are available to customers. Those kinds of setups have caught the attention of U.S. regulators, which have been examining potential conflicts of interest in recent years following the 2022 collapse of crypto exchange FTX and its Alameda Research trading arm.

The FTX implosion highlighted the crypto firm’s entanglements between in-house trading and its exchange. Those functions are generally kept separate in traditional financial markets—stock exchanges, for example, typically don’t own the market makers trading on them. More recently, the CFTC has included prediction markets in that scrutiny. 

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees prediction markets including Kalshi and Polymarket US, is now seeking comments on proposed rules aimed at preventing exchanges from giving affiliated trading firms an advantage over customers. They would require trading and exchange businesses to operate independently and would bar the trading firms from making speculative bets against customers.

“It’s really to address a different type of market structure that’s being used by crypto and prediction markets,” said Gabe Rosenberg, a partner at Davis Polk who advises financial institutions. “It’s about how many functions in the market can be done by one affiliated group and what protections need to be in place.”

Though the rules would apply across U.S. derivatives markets, the CFTC highlighted prediction markets as an area with recent “practical significance.” The agency said it knows of at least six exchanges that allow trading by affiliated firms, which can be a significant source of liquidity for prediction markets. 

The CFTC comment period ends in early October, after which the agency could revise the proposal and move toward final rules. For now, some of the most popular prediction markets say their setups provide a level playing field for customers, and any affiliated trading firms are market makers that provide liquidity so contracts can trade easily.

In the case of Polymarket, a company spokesperson said it doesn’t have its own market maker, either for its U.S. platform or for its separate, blockchain-based platform for international users. 

Kalshi, which is the biggest U.S. prediction market and is close to raising fresh cash at a $40 billion valuation, operates its own exchange and also owns Kalshi Trading, which trades on that exchange. A Kalshi spokesperson said the company supports the CFTC’s efforts.

“Kalshi Trading is unprofitable and represents a very small percentage of our volume. This is a very common and regulated practice in our industry,” the spokesperson said. Kalshi Trading doesn’t receive preferential treatment and doesn’t share personnel, office space or communication channels with Kalshi, the spokesperson said. 

“Like any financial market, including the stock market, market makers are industry standard because they help bootstrap liquidity,” the Kalshi spokesperson said. Institutional market makers, including outside trading firms as well as Kalshi Trading, represent less than 5% of volume on the exchange’s most liquid contracts, the spokesperson said. 

Robinhood until recently relied on outside exchanges, including Kalshi’s. items.summary:
Before we get to today’s column, we’re just three weeks away from AI Agenda Live, our flagship conference on all things artificial intelligence (a.k.a. my personal Super Bowl). 

We’ll be joined in San Francisco by top researchers, founders, operators and investors who will be answering all of our burning questions about what’s coming up in bleeding-edge AI research, the next breakthrough AI use cases, and how AI startups are thinking about competing with their biggest model suppliers. 

Speakers include Google DeepMind SVP & Chief AI Architect Koray Kavukcuoglu, who will be doing one of his first public interviews following the recent Google leadership shakeup, and OpenAI’s head of core products Thibault Sottiaux, who will be chatting about the ChatGPT maker’s product roadmap. You can’t miss it!
